Nested comparisons with uncfam_general()

George Kachergis

2026-11-06

Source: vignettes/nested-comparisons.Rmd
nested-comparisons.Rmd

The biased associative model of Kachergis, Yu & Shiffrin (2012), uncfam(), has several extensions in this package. uncfam_general() is one model with each extension as a parameter, so the variants are special cases of it:

uncfam_general() setting Equivalent to What it adds
defaults uncfam() attention to pairs by familiarity × uncertainty
B = 0 uncfam(B = 0) familiarity only
gamma = 0 uncfam(variant = "uncertainty-only") uncertainty only
uncertainty = "novelty" uncfam(variant = "novelty") novelty in place of entropy
gamma free uncfam_gamma() how strongly familiarity drives attention
eps free uncfam_elimination() learning by elimination (mutual exclusivity)
kappa = 1 uncfam_attention() more learning on more uncertain trials
K finite uncfam_sampling() attend to K sampled objects per word
rho > 0 (none) a short-term trace: recent pairings draw attention

These aren’t approximations: uncfam() and the other variants are implemented as calls to the same model, and give identical results.

d <- xsl_datasets[[1]]
identical(xsl_run(uncfam(X = .2, B = 3, C = .97), d)$fits[[1]]$perf,
          xsl_run(uncfam_general(X = .2, B = 3, C = .97), d)$fits[[1]]$perf)
#> [1] TRUE

Because the variants are nested, they can be compared directly. Does freeing a parameter improve the fit enough to justify it?

What the extensions do

Elimination (eps). A pair gains weight to the extent that the trial’s other words and objects are already accounted for by each other. Here word 2 is learned first, then appears with novel word 1. Elimination says object 1 must be word 1’s:

elim_data <- xslData(train = list(words = list(2, 2, c(1, 2), c(1, 3)),
                                  objects = list(2, 2, c(1, 2), c(1, 3))))
sapply(c(eps_0 = 0, eps_2 = 2, eps_10 = 10), \(e)
  xsl_run(uncfam_general(X = 1, B = 1, C = 1, eps = e), elim_data)$fits[[1]]$perf)
#>       eps_0     eps_2    eps_10
#> 1 0.7513276 0.9538716 0.9681789
#> 2 0.9892157 0.9898250 0.9900613
#> 3 0.5338423 0.9449978 0.9684734

Short-term trace (rho, Cs). Every update also goes into a second matrix that decays quickly (by Cs per trial), and attention follows familiarity plus rho times this trace. Here word 1 meets object 1 twice, then object 2 twice, then both together. Without a trace the two objects end level; with one, the more recent pairing pulls ahead:

trace_data <- xslData(train = list(words = list(1, 1, 1, 1, 1),
                                   objects = list(1, 1, 2, 2, c(1, 2))))
sapply(c(rho_0 = 0, rho_5 = 5), \(r)
  xsl_run(uncfam_general(X = .5, B = 0, C = 1, rho = r, Cs = .5), trace_data)$fits[[1]]$matrix[1, ])
#>   rho_0    rho_5
#> 1  1.26 1.155173
#> 2  1.26 1.364827

Sampled attention (K). With a finite K, each word attends to K objects drawn in proportion to familiarity × uncertainty, so the model is stochastic. xsl_run() averages xslControl(n_sim = ) simulated learners:

set.seed(1)
xsl_run(uncfam_general(X = .2, B = 3, C = .97, K = 1), d, xslControl(n_sim = 50))$sse
#> [1] 1.886384

A nested comparison

Does freeing the familiarity exponent gamma improve on the original model? The comparison below fits both, by binomial likelihood, to two conditions: 212 (a 4AFC test) and 301 (24 words).

Two precautions keep the comparison fair. First, the larger model’s search starts from the smaller model’s best fit (with gamma = 1), so it can’t fit worse merely because its search got unlucky. Second, the search uses a fixed seed.

labels <- vapply(xsl_datasets, `[[`, "", "label")
ctrl <- xslControl(objective = "binomial", lapse = .02)

fit_nested <- function(data, free, lower, upper, start = NULL) {
  np <- 30
  pop <- NULL
  if (!is.null(start)) {
    set.seed(2)
    pop <- sapply(seq_along(lower), \(j) stats::runif(np, lower[j], upper[j]))
    pop[1, ] <- start
  }
  xsl_fit(uncfam_general(X = .1, B = 1, C = 1), data, lower = lower, upper = upper,
          free = free, control = ctrl, seed = 1,
          deoptim_control = DEoptim::DEoptim.control(NP = np, itermax = 25, trace = FALSE,
                                                     initialpop = pop))[[1]]
}

compare_gamma <- function(label) {
  data <- xsl_datasets[[which(labels == label)]]
  bam <- fit_nested(data, c("X", "B", "C"), c(.001, .1, .5), c(5, 15, 1))
  gam <- fit_nested(data, c("X", "B", "C", "gamma"), c(.001, .1, .5, 0), c(5, 15, 1, 6),
                    start = c(bam$optim$bestmem, gamma = 1))
  lr <- 2 * (gam$loglik - bam$loglik)
  data.frame(condition = label, gamma = gam$optim$bestmem[["gamma"]],
             delta_AIC = gam$aic - bam$aic, LR = lr,
             p = stats::pchisq(lr, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
}
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("212", "301"), compare_gamma))
res
#>   condition      gamma  delta_AIC        LR            p
#> 1       212 2.81229618 -9.3590162 11.359016 0.0007508258
#> 2       301 0.04337925 -0.8448739  2.844874 0.0916657856

The two conditions pull gamma in opposite directions:

  • In 212, familiarity is amplified (gamma = 2.8, p = 7.5^{-4}). Pairs that are already familiar draw even more attention.
  • In 301, it is nearly switched off (gamma = 0.04). Attention follows uncertainty alone. The improvement here is smaller (p = 0.092).

A single gamma fit across many conditions would average these. Fitting the nested variants condition by condition can reveal such differences, where a single group fit hides them.

Two caveats:

  • The p-values are approximate. The binomial treats every response as independent, which overstates the evidence. And for parameters whose null value sits on a bound, such as eps = 0 or kappa = 0, the chi-square p-value is conservative.
  • Small conditions can’t tell variants apart. With only 8 to 24 test items per condition, several parameters are weakly identified.
